questions.question_text: How loud and resonant does this language sound when spoken?

options.text: Like a pure, breathless whisper with no throat vibration.
Soft and hushed, mostly using air rather than loud voice.
Normal conversational volume, mixing soft and vibrating sounds.
Strong and resonant, with clear chest vibration.
Booming, loud, and dramatic, with musical pitch changes in the voice.

questions.question_text: Does the language flow smoothly like a song, or does it have sharp stops and clicks?

options.text: Very choppy and percussive, full of sharp clicks, air stops, and harsh consonant clusters.
Rhythmic and crisp, with frequent hard consonants and occasional throat stops.
Balanced rhythm between consonants and vowels.
Smooth and poetic, avoiding harsh consonant collisions.
Purely melodic and liquid, almost entirely made of vowels and soft flowing sounds.

questions.question_text: Which part of the mouth do speakers use the most to form their words?

options.text: Right at the front of the lips and teeth, with bright vowels (like i and e).
Mostly near the front of the mouth and tip of the tongue.
Evenly distributed across the lips, tongue, and throat.
Towards the back of the mouth, with deeper vowels (like o and u).
Deep in the throat, guttural and dark, with heavy back-of-the-throat sounds.

questions.question_text: When you look at a page written in this language, how long are the words?

options.text: Tiny, one-syllable words that never attach to each other.
Short words with only an occasional simple ending.
Medium-sized words, similar to English or Spanish.
Long words that glue multiple prefixes, suffixes, and nouns together.
Massive words where an entire sentence gets packed into a single giant word.

questions.question_text: How regular and predictable are the grammar rules when modifying a word?

options.text: 100% logical like Lego blocks: endings snap on cleanly with strict vowel harmony and zero exceptions.
Very regular and harmonious, with almost no irregular words.
Moderately regular, with a few common irregular words.
Words often mutate on the inside when conjugated, with several ancient exceptions.
Ancient and chaotic: word roots constantly change their internal vowels and many words break the rules.

questions.question_text: When speakers describe an event, where do they put the action (the verb) in the sentence?

options.text: Right at the very beginning of the sentence to grab attention immediately (Action -> Actor -> Target).
Usually near the start, leading with action and prepositions.
Right in the middle of the sentence, between the actor and the target (like English).
Towards the end, setting up the people and objects first.
Strictly at the very end of the sentence, saving the action for the final climax (Actor -> Target -> Action).

questions.question_text: Can speakers move words around freely in a sentence for poetic effect, or must words stay in a strict order?

options.text: Strict word order is mandatory, using small helper words ('the', 'to', 'of') instead of noun endings.
Mostly fixed order with common helper particles.
Balanced: uses a few noun endings for subject/object and some helper words.
Flexible order: special suffixes on nouns show who did what, reducing the need for helper words.
Total poetic freedom: nouns carry rich case endings so words can be placed in any order.

questions.question_text: Does the grammar divide objects and living things into special categories or genders?

options.text: No categories at all: nouns and adjectives never change for gender or class.
Simple masculine/feminine split, but without changing the adjectives much.
Classic 2 or 3 genders where adjectives match the noun.
Divides the world by soul/animacy (humans, animals, tools, nature) with visible prefixes.
Obsessive classification by physical shape and soul (round, flat, long, liquid, living), marking every noun and adjective.

questions.question_text: How does this language invent words for complex things like 'tear', 'volcano', or 'wisdom'?

options.text: By combining poetic nature and body words literally (e.g., 'eye-water' for tear, 'fire-mountain' for volcano).
Mostly through physical metaphors and nature combinations.
An equal mix of poetic compound words and independent vocabulary.
Mostly by creating unique roots and adding academic suffixes.
Purely abstract and scientific: every concept gets its own unique root word and specialized suffixes (-ism, -ology).

questions.question_text: How strictly do verbs track time (past, present, future) and whether an action is finished?

options.text: Verbs never change for time; speakers just add standalone words like 'yesterday' if needed.
Minimal verb changes, relying mostly on context and time words.
Standard past, present, and future verb endings.
Detailed verb endings that mark both time and whether the action is continuous or habitual.
Hyper-precise timeline: verbs must mark exact temporal distance (remote past, mythic time) and completion state.

questions.question_text: Does the grammar force speakers to prove how they know a piece of information?

options.text: Never: you state facts directly without marking if you saw it or heard a rumor.
Only basic markers for certainty or doubt.
Moderate: verbs mark wishes and possibilities, with optional source markers.
Strict: verbs require a suffix showing if you witnessed the event directly or heard it second-hand.
Mandatory truth-tracking: every verb must carry suffixes proving if it was seen, heard as rumor, deduced from clues, or remembered.

questions.question_text: Does the language change depending on the social rank or status of the person you are talking to?

options.text: Total equality: everyone uses the exact same pronouns and verbs whether speaking to a beggar or a ruler.
Mostly equal, with only minor polite expressions.
Has a polite/formal 'you' and 'I' for strangers or elders.
Strong hierarchy: verbs take honorific suffixes and pronouns change by social class.
Strict caste system: completely different pronouns and separate royal/commoner vocabulary for everyday actions.

questions.question_text: What physical tools and surfaces were used to create this language's writing system?

options.text: Chiseled into hard stone or carved into wood with a knife (straight lines and sharp angles only).
Pressed into clay or scratched onto bark with angular strokes.
Written with a standard pen on parchment, balancing straight lines and curves.
Inscribed on delicate palm leaves with a stylus, using rounded shapes to avoid tearing the leaf.
Painted with a soft ink brush on silk or paper in long, flowing, unbroken calligraphic curves.

questions.question_text: What does a single written symbol represent in this writing system?

options.text: A single basic letter/sound (a simple, compact Alphabet).
Mostly single sounds with slightly more ornate letter shapes.
A complete syllable joining a consonant and a vowel (a Syllabary).
Complex syllable blocks with multiple strokes per character.
An entire word or concept per symbol (intricate Logograms / Hieroglyphs).
